analysis.title: Capital Market Outlook, November 16, 2026
key_insights: Real U.S. GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in Q3, led by 3.8% real consumer spending growth, AI-related business investment and a 16% annualized rise in real federal government spending. The prior three quarters averaged 1.6%.

Year-over-year, GDP and consumption growth are about 2.1% and 2.5%, which the CIO does not regard as exceptional. Business surveys (ISM, NFIB, Beige Book) point to moderate growth. ISM manufacturing is strong, ISM services is lagging.

October payrolls rose 165,000 and prior months were revised up. The three-month average is 137,000, up from 28,000 in July. Unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.5% in November 2025. The CIO says part of the gain is catch-up from the post-tariff hiring lull.

Labor force participation has rebounded since July, bringing nearly 1.6 million people back into the labor force. The CIO argues this, plus solid productivity, limits wage and unit-labor-cost pressure, so renewed hiring need not be inflationary.

Stronger hiring and a higher-than-expected October CPI revived expectations of further Fed tightening and pushed rates sharply higher. The CIO warns that higher rates could restrain demand and delay housing, power generation and other capacity investment needed to ease inflation.

Several supports to Q3 growth look unsustainable: a weaker AI investment impulse after the midterms and base effects, inventory accumulation that cannot continue, and a saving rate that fell from 6.2% in January to 3.8% in September. BofA Global Research expects growth of about 2.3% ahead.

Core CPI stayed faster than desired in October with some broadening. Shelter accounted for about a third of the October core increase and housing-services inflation is near its prepandemic average, so the disinflation tailwind is fading. Brent fell from roughly $135 to $95 per barrel in recent weeks, but diesel and freight costs still feed into other prices.

Structural inflation pressures the CIO lists: electricity costs, infrastructure bottlenecks, skilled-labor shortages, an aging population, housing supply, inflation-insensitive wealthy households, trade and industrial policy, and AI-investment resource demand. These matter if accommodated by large fiscal deficits, excess credit growth or a wage-cost spiral.

The S&P 500 is up less than 1% since early June. Breadth deteriorated: by end of September nearly 60% of constituents were more than 15% below their 52-week closing highs. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell as much as 38% from its mid-June peak through early November and is still about 31% below it.

With about 91% of S&P 500 companies reported as of November 13, Q3 EPS growth is tracking about 32% y/y per FactSet. That would be a third straight quarter above 25% and an eighth straight quarter of double-digit growth. Revenue growth is double-digit and the Q3 net margin is tracking its second-highest since 2009.

Markets are reacting weakly to earnings. Companies beating on both EPS and sales outperformed the S&P 500 by 90 bp the next day versus a 1.4 percentage point average. Companies missing on both traded roughly in line versus an average 2.5 point underperformance. The beat-miss gap is the narrowest since Q4 2000 and Q4 2001.
BofA Global Research expects S&P 500 EPS growth to slow from 33% in 2026 to 12% in 2027. Bottom-up consensus is higher at 16%.

Technology and Energy account for about 75% of Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth. BofA Global Research estimates a 20% cut to 2027 AI capex would mean 35% to 40% downside to AI semiconductor EPS and about 7% to 8% lower S&P 500 EPS before secondary effects. Hyperscalers have so far kept raising capex plans.
Midterm results are a new uncertainty for the AI investment cycle: newly elected Democratic governors in several data-center states have supported tighter development restrictions.

Breadth of earnings beats is wide: 84% of S&P 500 companies beat mean EPS estimates versus a five-year average of 78%, and nine of 11 sectors have 80% or more beating. Atlanta Fed GDPNow tracks 3.5% for Q4. Bank of America card spending per household rose 5.8% y/y in October (4.6% excluding gasoline).

China's merchandise trade surplus reached $1T in the first 10 months of 2026 and is on track for about $1.3T for the year, roughly triple the 2019 level of $421B. The U.S. share of China's exports fell from 20% in 2019 to 10% now, down from 15% before Liberation Day.

Trade pushback against China is spreading (EU EV quotas, Indian anti-dumping probes, tariffs in Mexico, Brazil and South Africa). The CIO expects more targeted tariffs and subsidies in 2027 but not a full global trade war, and expects U.S. tariffs to stay via Section 232 and 301 despite the Democratic midterm sweep.

Portfolio stance: overweight equities and U.S. stocks. The CIO sees conditions building for a year-end rally and views recent sharp declines in Financials, parts of Industrials, higher-quality semiconductors and power generation as potentially overdone. It favors extending duration out of cash and the front end, with the 10-year near 5% and real yields above 2.5%.

sector_views.rationale: Supportive fundamentals, record margins and rising productivity. Weakness is to be used to rebalance.
Recent sharp declines are viewed as potentially overdone, in the context of the CIO's overall constructive equity stance.
Parts of Industrials are seen as oversold. The CIO also sees opportunity in cyclical sectors and broader participation.
Higher-quality semiconductors are called potentially oversold after a roughly 31% drawdown in the SOX, but the CIO stresses diversification and quality given AI capex risk.
Recent sharp declines in power generation are viewed as potentially overdone.

earnings_insights: S&P 500 Q3 2026 EPS growth is tracking about 32% y/y blended per FactSet (reported results for about 91% of companies as of 11/13 plus estimates for the rest).
84% of reporting S&P 500 companies beat mean EPS estimates per FactSet, versus a five-year average of 78%. Nine of 11 sectors have 80% or more beating.
BofA Global Research projects S&P 500 EPS growth of 33% in 2026 and 12% in 2027. Bottom-up consensus for 2027 is 16%.
Technology and Energy contributed about 75% of Q3 S&P 500 EPS growth (FactSet, blended).

Next-day reaction to reported results has been muted: double beats outperformed the index by 90 bp versus a 1.4 point historical average. Double misses were in line versus a 2.5 point historical underperformance.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Strong, boosted by inventories, AI investment and federal spending. Year-over-year growth is about 2.1%.
Spending barely rose in September after an August spike and is outpacing income as the saving rate falls.
Down from 6.2% in January, which limits how long spending can outpace income.
Beat expectations. Three-month average is 137,000 versus 28,000 in July.
Down from 4.5% in November 2025. Average duration of unemployment is at a five-year high.
Revived expectations for further Fed tightening. Core CPI broadened, with shelter about a third of the core increase.
Real-time model estimate showing above-trend growth continuing.

trade_ideas.description: Extend duration: move out of cash and the front end of the Treasury curve into longer maturities, with the 10-year near 5% and real yields above 2.5%
trade_ideas.rationale: Higher yields offer attractive income and diversification.

trade_ideas.description: Buy weakness in Financials, parts of Industrials, higher-quality semiconductors and power generation, and rebalance into equities
trade_ideas.rationale: The CIO views the recent sharp declines as potentially overdone, with a supportive fundamental backdrop.
trade_ideas.risk: A cut to AI capex after the midterms. BofA Global Research estimates a 20% cut to 2027 AI capex would lower S&P 500 EPS by about 7% to 8%.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight U.S. equities relative to Europe on the view that U.S. growth is less exposed to Chinese manufactured exports
trade_ideas.rationale: The U.S. economy is diversified, services-led and already protected by tariffs.
trade_ideas.risk: Competition from China on U.S. technology supremacy.

risk_factors: Oil market developments, including the diesel and freight pass-through to other prices.
A slowdown in AI investment after the midterms. A 20% cut to 2027 AI capex would mean 35% to 40% downside to AI semiconductor EPS and 7% to 8% lower S&P 500 EPS.
Further Fed tightening that overly restrains demand and delays housing, power and capacity investment.
Slower growth as inventory, AI investment and federal spending tailwinds fade and the saving rate falls.
Limited room for further margin expansion from historically elevated levels.
Earnings growth is concentrated: Technology and Energy account for about 75% of Q3 growth.
Structural inflation pressures from electricity costs, infrastructure bottlenecks, skilled-labor shortages, an aging population, housing supply and large fiscal deficits.
Competition from China on U.S. technology supremacy.
Escalating global trade restrictions on China-linked manufactured goods.
vol_and_positioning: Market breadth deteriorated through the summer: by end of September nearly 60% of S&P 500 constituents were more than 15% below their 52-week closing highs, while the index was roughly flat.
Leadership rotated in October and November: mega-cap Technology came under pressure while previously lagging areas recovered.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell as much as 38% from its mid-June peak through early November and remains about 31% below it.
The S&P 500 is in a sideways range since early June, up less than 1%.
The CIO's view is that conditions for a year-end rally are building as focus shifts from volatility and rotation to growth, margins and productivity.
geopolitical: Geopolitical conflicts are keeping diesel prices elevated, and diesel could decline once they resolve.
Brent oil moved from roughly $135 to $95 per barrel in recent weeks, and oil market developments remain an important risk.
China's $1T trade surplus is prompting pushback: EU electric vehicle import quotas, Indian anti-dumping investigations, and product-specific tariffs in Mexico, Brazil and South Africa.
U.S. tariffs are expected to stay through Section 232 and Section 301 measures despite the Democratic sweep at the midterms.
A full tit-for-tat global trade war in 2027 is not the base case.
cross_bank_references: Bank of America Global Research expects S&P 500 EPS growth of 12% in 2027 versus bottom-up consensus of 16%.

tension_points.bull_case: Moderate growth, solid productivity and rising labor supply can let inflation moderate as tariff and oil effects fade, which reduces the risk of a hard landing from aggressive Fed tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: Strong Q3 growth, a 4.1% unemployment rate and hot October CPI with broadening core have revived expectations of more tightening. Structural supply constraints could keep inflation elevated if fiscal deficits, credit growth or wealth effects accommodate them.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Core CPI that keeps running above the Fed's target as shelter's disinflation tailwind fades, or diesel prices that stay elevated after geopolitical conflicts.

tension_points.bull_case: EPS growth is tracking about 32% in Q3, 84% of companies beat estimates, and hyperscalers keep raising capex plans. Conditions for a broad earnings downturn are largely absent.
tension_points.bear_case: Growth is concentrated in Technology and Energy (about 75%), the 2027 comparison base is hard, and midterm outcomes may bring tighter data-center restrictions. A 20% cut to 2027 AI capex would lower S&P 500 EPS by about 7% to 8%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in AI capex guidance from hyperscalers, which has not yet appeared.

theme_stances.key_argument: Earnings growth will moderate but a broader downturn is not yet indicated, so the focus should be on where growth comes from and how durable it is.
theme_stances.evidence: the broader backdrop does not yet point to a fundamental downturn

theme_stances.theme: Fed tightening risk to supply response
theme_stances.key_argument: Restrictive interest rates may delay the supply response needed to ease some inflation pressures.
theme_stances.evidence: Restrictive interest rates may in fact delay the very supply response

theme_stances.theme: China export surplus and global tariffs
theme_stances.key_argument: China's export-led model will keep drawing targeted trade barriers in 2027, though a full global trade war is not the base case.
theme_stances.evidence: a full-blown tit-for-tat global trade war is far from our base case
